Use the Weave documentation at https://docs.wandb.ai/weave to answer this question:

How do tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together?
output.answer:
**Short answer:** Tracing gives you the record of what your agent did. Evaluations and Signals both score behavior, but at different points. Evaluations run your model or function against a dataset you define. Signals score production traces automatically. The docs describe these pieces separately, so the combined loop at the end is my inference.

**Tracing (the record).** For agents, Weave's Agents view is the trace view. It gives a turn-by-turn record of each conversation, including token usage, tool invocations and execution spans [S4].

**Evaluations (structured measurement).** An `Evaluation` object is a blueprint. It defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions [S2].
- Running `.evaluate()` runs a `Model` or custom function against that blueprint. This is an evaluation run [S2].
- The purpose is to measure performance on repeatable cases, compare changes over time and find regressions [S2].
- Scorers are the scoring functions. They take the AI's output and return a dictionary of results, and you pass them to a `weave.Evaluation` [S7].

**Signals (production scoring).** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. They flag quality and safety issues and highlight the traces that need attention [S1, S4].
- A rating is a 0.0–1.0 score on a span. Tags are labels such as "user-frustration" [S3].
- An older docs page says every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored. Its note says new implementations should use Signals under Weave for Agents [S5].
- That page also says the scores and failure analyses help you identify weaknesses to act on [S5].

**Likely loop (inference):**
1. Trace your agent.
2. Use Signals to surface problem conversations.
3. In a conversation's details, use **Add to dataset** to save messages to a `Dataset` [S6].
4. Use that dataset as test examples in an `Evaluation` to check that a fix helps [S2].

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# View agent activity

> Use Weave's Agents view to understand what your agent did, how much it cost, and exactly where things went right or wrong.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/conversations/view-activity.md).

The Agents view gives you a turn-by-turn record of every conversation your agent had, along with token usage, tool invocations, and execution spans.

Agent applications are hard to debug because the interesting behavior happens between the user's request and the final response. The Agents view in Weave makes that middle layer visible. Every conversation your agent had is captured here, with the full message history, span-level execution detail, and token costs attached. You can see at a glance whether an agent completed its task, how many tool calls it made, and where time or budget was spent. For teams building and iterating on agents, this is the starting point for understanding behavior in production.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

# Scoring overview

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

**Python**

Pass Scorers to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation. Weave supports two types of Scorers:

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.
2. **Class-based Scorers:** Python classes that inherit from `weave.Scorer` for more complex evaluations.

Scorers must return a dictionary and can return multiple metrics, nested metrics, and non-numeric values such as text returned from an LLM-evaluator about its reasoning.

**TypeScript**

Scorers are special ops that you pass to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.

# Scoring overview

> Evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics with Weave Scorers

In Weave, Scorers evaluate AI outputs and return evaluation metrics. They take the AI's output, analyze it, and return a dictionary of results. Scorers can use your input data as reference if needed and can also output extra information, such as explanations or reasoning from the evaluation.

This guide is for developers who want to measure the quality of their AI system's outputs. It explains how Scorers fit into Weave evaluations, how to build your own Scorers, how to apply Scorers to individual calls, and how to analyze the resulting scores.

**Python**

Pass Scorers to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation. Weave supports two types of Scorers:

1. **Function-based Scorers:** Python functions decorated with `@weave.op`.
2. **Class-based Scorers:** Python classes that inherit from `weave.Scorer` for more complex evaluations.

Scorers must return a dictionary and can return multiple metrics, nested metrics, and non-numeric values such as text returned from an LLM-evaluator about its reasoning.

**TypeScript**

Scorers are special ops that you pass to a `weave.Evaluation` object during evaluation.

**Short answer:** Tracing records what your application or agent did. Evaluations measure it against repeatable test cases. Signals score and tag live agent activity. The first is the data, and the other two are ways of judging it. The docs don't present the three in one combined workflow, so the grouping below is my inference from the separate pages.

- **Tracing (the record):** Weave's Agents view gives a turn-by-turn record of each agent conversation. It includes token usage, tool invocations and execution spans [S4]. Signals use these same traces. The Agent Lens note says it "uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave" [S1].
- **Evaluations (pre-release testing):** An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The docs say this lets you measure performance on repeatable cases, compare changes over time and find regressions [S2].
- **Signals (production monitoring):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. These flag quality and safety issues, such as poor responses, user frustration or NSFW content, and they highlight the traces that need attention [S1, S4]. A rating is a 0.0–1.0 score on a span, and tags are labels such as "user-frustration" [S3].

**How they connect (inference):**
1. Trace your agent. This gives you the conversations and spans.
2. Use Signals to score those production traces automatically and find problem cases.
3. The Agents view lets you add agent messages to a dataset. That could feed an `Evaluation` dataset, but I haven't confirmed that workflow in the docs.
4. Use evaluations to check that a fix improves results on those cases.

Signals and evaluations both score outputs. Evaluations score a fixed dataset on demand, while Signals score traces from your running agent.

## Available signals

Weave offers monitors with built-in signals: preset scorers that evaluate production traces for common quality issues and errors by default, with no custom setup. Each built-in signal uses a benchmarked LLM prompt to classify traces and saves the results as comma-delimited tags representing the detected issues.

Signals use a [Serverless Inference](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/inference/serverless.md) model to score traces, so you don't need external API keys.

Weave provides 13 preset signals organized into two groups.

## Signals and custom monitors

Use [signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/monitors.md), preset automated scorers for production traces, to get started with production monitoring quickly, then add custom monitors for evaluation criteria specific to your application.

| | Signals | Custom monitors |
| - | - | - |
| **Configuration** | One-click enable, no prompt writing | Full control over scoring prompt, model, and parameters |
| **Scope** | Preset quality and error classifiers | Any evaluation criteria you define |
| **Trace selection** | Automatic (successful root traces for quality, failed traces for errors) | Configurable operations, filters, and sampling rate |
| **Model** | Serverless Inference (preset) | Any commercial or Serverless Inference model |
| **Use case** | Quick production monitoring with proven classifiers | Custom evaluation criteria specific to your application |

# Overview

> Practical guides and examples for building with Weights & Biases Weave

Welcome to the W\&B Weave cookbook collection. These hands-on guides provide practical examples and best practices for building applications with Weave. Use this page to browse cookbooks by topic and jump into the example that matches what you're trying to build.

> **[Getting started](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/cookbooks/Intro_to_Weave_Hello_Trace.md)**
>
> Start with Weave through practical, hands-on examples covering tracing and evaluation basics.

> **[Evaluations and datasets](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/cookbooks/leaderboard_quickstart.md)**

# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

**Short answer:** Tracing records what your application or agent did. Evaluations measure it against repeatable test cases. Signals score and tag live agent activity. The first is the data, and the other two are ways of judging it. The docs don't present the three in one combined workflow, so the grouping below is my inference from the separate pages.

- **Tracing (the record):** Weave's Agents view gives a turn-by-turn record of each agent conversation. It includes token usage, tool invocations and execution spans [S4]. Signals use these same traces. The Agent Lens note says it "uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave" [S1].
- **Evaluations (pre-release testing):** An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset of test examples and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run. The docs say this lets you measure performance on repeatable cases, compare changes over time and find regressions [S2].
- **Signals (production monitoring):** In the Agents view, the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. These flag quality and safety issues, such as poor responses, user frustration or NSFW content, and they highlight the traces that need attention [S1, S4]. A rating is a 0.0–1.0 score on a span, and tags are labels such as "user-frustration" [S3].

**How they connect (inference):**
1. Trace your agent. This gives you the conversations and spans.
2. Use Signals to score those production traces automatically and find problem cases.
3. The Agents view lets you add agent messages to a dataset. That could feed an `Evaluation` dataset, but I haven't confirmed that workflow in the docs.
4. Use evaluations to check that a fix improves results on those cases.

Signals and evaluations both score outputs. Evaluations score a fixed dataset on demand, while Signals score traces from your running agent.

# Monitor using built-in signals

> Weights & Biases provides built-in scoring solutions for agents in production

> [!NOTE]
>
> This page covers a previous approach to monitoring production traffic. For new implementations, use **Signals** under Weave for Agents. See [View agent signals](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

Standard system metrics like latency, token count, and cost don't fully capture agent behavior. Inspecting individual traces provides deep insight but doesn't scale to the millions of traces generated in a live environment.

Signals provide a high-level monitoring solution to this problem by offering automated, behavioral scoring for agents in production:

* Automated scoring: Every incoming production trace is automatically processed and scored on common quality issues and errors.
* Infrastructure: Processing is powered by CoreWeave compute and CoreWeave GPUs for scalability across millions of traces.

By using signals within production, you can:

* Gain behavioral insight. Move beyond system metrics to understand if your agent is hallucinating, failing to follow conversation patterns, or losing grounding in its evidence.
* Accelerate the research loop. Use the scores and failure analyses generated by signals to identify weaknesses, which you can use to research model improvement, data annotation, or reinforcement learning.
